questions.q: What is the basic four-chain polypeptide monomer structure of an immunoglobulin molecule?
options: Two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains
One heavy chain and three light chains
Two alpha chains and two beta chains
questions.explain: A standard monomeric immunoglobulin consists of two identical heavy chains (~50-70 kDa) and two identical light chains (~25 kDa) held together by interchain disulfide bonds and non-covalent interactions, forming a Y-shaped molecule with two antigen-binding (Fab) regions and one crystallizable (Fc) stem.

open.q: How many heavy chains and how many light chains make up a standard immunoglobulin monomer?
accept: Two heavy chains and two light chains

questions.q: Which two light-chain isotypes exist in human immunoglobulins, and how are they distributed within a single antibody molecule?
options: Alpha and beta chains, both in one antibody
Two kappa chains or two lambda chains, but not a mixture
Gamma and mu chains in each Fab arm
Epsilon and delta chains linked only by peptide bonds
questions.explain: Humans have kappa and lambda light chains (~60% kappa and ~40% lambda in serum); within any single immunoglobulin molecule, both light chains are of the same isotype (either both kappa or both lambda).

open.q: Name the two light-chain isotypes found in human immunoglobulins.

questions.q: Which human immunoglobulin class (isotype) is the most abundant in normal adult serum (~70-75% of total serum Ig), crosses the placenta via FcRn, and provides secondary immune memory?
questions.explain: IgG is the predominant serum immunoglobulin, has a long serum half-life (~21 days for IgG1/IgG2/IgG4 due to neonatal Fc receptor [FcRn] recycling), activates complement (IgG1, IgG3), opsonizes microbes, and is the only class actively transported across the placenta.

open.q: Which immunoglobulin class is the most abundant in human serum and crosses the placenta?

questions.q: Which immunoglobulin class is the primary antibody of mucosal secretions (saliva, tears, colostrum, breast milk, respiratory and intestinal mucus) and exists as a dimer joined by a J-chain with a secretory component?
questions.explain: Secretory IgA (sIgA) is transported across epithelial cells via the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor (pIgR), retaining a cleaved portion of the receptor called the secretory component that shields it from proteolytic digestion in mucosal secretions.

open.q: Name the polypeptide attached to secretory IgA during epithelial transcytosis that protects it from proteolysis in mucosal secretions.

questions.q: Why is pentameric IgM (joined by a J-chain) particularly efficient at activating the classical complement pathway despite having lower affinity per individual binding site than affinity-matured IgG?
options: Multivalent IgM engages multiple C1q heads when bound to antigen
It crosses the placenta in high concentrations
It binds directly to mast-cell Fc-epsilon-RI receptors
questions.explain: Activating C1q requires binding at least two globular heads of the C1q hexamer; a single pentameric IgM molecule bound to multivalent surface antigens can engage C1q effectively, whereas monomeric IgG requires multiple closely spaced IgG molecules.

open.q: Which complement subcomponent binds to the Fc region of antigen-complexed IgM or IgG to initiate the classical complement pathway?

questions.q: Which immunoglobulin class mediates Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity and allergic reactions by binding high-affinity Fc-epsilon-RI receptors on tissue mast cells and blood basophils?
questions.explain: IgE has the lowest serum concentration and shortest free half-life (~2 days), but cell-bound IgE on mast cells/basophils persists for weeks to months; cross-linking of bound IgE by multivalent allergen triggers degranulation and release of histamine, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins.

open.q: Which immunoglobulin class binds Fc-epsilon-RI on mast cells and basophils to mediate immediate allergic reactions?

questions.q: Which immunoglobulin isotype is co-expressed with surface IgM on the membrane of mature naive B lymphocytes as a B-cell antigen receptor (BCR)?
questions.explain: Naive mature B cells display membrane-bound IgM and IgD on their surface, sharing identical antigen specificity via alternative splicing of VDJ to either C-mu or C-delta heavy-chain exons.

open.q: Which membrane immunoglobulin is co-expressed with IgM on mature naive B cells?

questions.q: How does papain digestion of an IgG molecule differ from pepsin digestion?
options: Papain cleaves below the hinge region to yield two monovalent Fab fragments and one intact Fc fragment, whereas pepsin cleaves below the disulfide bonds in the hinge to yield one bivalent F(ab')2 fragment and degraded Fc peptides
Pepsin yields three identical Fab fragments
Papain separates heavy chains from light chains without cleaving peptide bonds
questions.explain: Papain cleaves N-terminal to the inter-heavy-chain disulfide bond (producing two Fab fragments and one Fc fragment), whereas pepsin cleaves C-terminal to the inter-chain disulfide bond, keeping both Fab arms linked as a bivalent F(ab')2 fragment while digesting the Fc region.

open.q: Which proteolytic enzyme cleaves IgG beneath the inter-heavy-chain hinge disulfide bond to leave a bivalent F(ab')2 fragment?

questions.q: Which enzymes (RAG1 and RAG2) initiate V(D)J recombination in developing B and T lymphocytes by introducing double-strand DNA breaks at recombination signal sequences (RSS)?
options: Recombination-activating gene proteins RAG1 and RAG2
questions.explain: RAG1 and RAG2 form the V(D)J recombinase complex that nicks DNA adjacent to heptamer-spacer-nonamer RSS elements and forms hairpin coding ends, which are then opened by Artemis and joined by non-homologous end joining (XRCC4, DNA ligase IV).

open.q: Name the two recombination-activating gene proteins that initiate V(D)J recombination in developing lymphocytes.

questions.q: How does terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) increase junctional diversity during V(D)J rearrangement?
options: Adds non-templated nucleotides at V(D)J coding junctions
Performs class switching in germinal centres
questions.explain: TdT adds random nucleotides without a template at coding joints during heavy- and light-chain rearrangement, creating extensive junctional diversity in the hypervariable CDR3 antigen-binding loop.

open.q: What enzyme adds non-templated N-nucleotides at V(D)J junctions to increase antibody and TCR diversity?

questions.q: Which enzyme is required for BOTH somatic hypermutation (affinity maturation) and class-switch recombination (isotype switching) in activated B cells within germinal centers?
questions.explain: AID deaminates cytosine (C) to uracil (U) in single-stranded DNA of immunoglobulin variable regions (driving somatic hypermutation and higher-affinity antibodies) and switch (S) regions (driving deletion/recombination to IgG, IgA, or IgE).

open.q: Name the enzyme that deaminates cytosine to uracil in immunoglobulin genes to drive somatic hypermutation and class-switch recombination.

questions.q: A 9-month-old boy presents with recurrent severe bacterial sinopulmonary infections, absent serum IgG, IgA, and IgE, elevated or normal serum IgM, and lymph node germinal centers lacking class-switched B cells. Mutation in the gene encoding which enzyme causes Hyper-IgM syndrome type 2 (HIGM2)?
questions.explain: Hyper-IgM syndrome can result from X-linked CD40L (CD154) deficiency on T cells, CD40 deficiency on B cells, or autosomal recessive AID (AICDA) / UNG deficiency, blocking class-switch recombination so B cells produce only IgM.

open.q: Which immunoglobulin class is typically elevated or normal while IgG, IgA, and IgE are markedly decreased in Hyper-IgM syndrome?

questions.q: Which non-covalent intermolecular forces mediate antigen-antibody binding at the paratope-epitope interface?
options: Hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions, hydrophobic forces and van der Waals forces
Covalent peptide bonds formed during each binding event
Phosphodiester bonds between antigen and Fab
Glycosidic bonds between heavy and light chains
questions.explain: Antigen-antibody binding is reversible and relies on complementary spatial topography enabling hydrogen bonding, electrostatic attractions, van der Waals contacts, and hydrophobic interactions (releasing ordered water molecules).

open.q: Are antigen-antibody interactions in physiological complexes primarily covalent or non-covalent?

questions.q: How does antibody affinity differ from antibody avidity?
options: Affinity: single-site strength; avidity: total multivalent binding strength
Avidity measures only T-cell receptor binding
Affinity applies only to pentameric IgM
questions.explain: A pentameric IgM molecule may have modest intrinsic affinity per binding site early in an immune response, but its ten sites give high functional avidity when binding multivalent pathogens.

open.q: What term describes the overall binding strength between a multivalent antibody and a multivalent antigen?

questions.q: What is cross-reactivity in immunochemistry?
options: Binding to a different antigen with a similar epitope
Simultaneous IgG and IgE synthesis by one plasma cell
questions.explain: Cross-reactivity occurs when two distinct antigens share identical or structurally similar epitopes (molecular mimicry), such as streptococcal M protein sharing epitopes with cardiac myosin in acute rheumatic fever.

open.q: What term describes the reaction of an antibody with a second antigen that shares structural similarity or a common epitope with the inducing antigen?

questions.q: What is a hapten?
options: A large protein that is immunogenic on its own
A small molecule that becomes immunogenic when linked to a carrier protein
A complement regulator on red cells
An MHC class I heavy chain
questions.explain: Haptens (such as dinitrophenol, urushiol in poison ivy, or penicillin metabolites) are antigenic (bind antibody) but not immunogenic alone because they lack the size/T-cell help needed to trigger adaptive activation without a carrier protein.

open.q: Name a small molecule that binds antibody specifically but requires covalent attachment to a carrier protein to induce an immune response.

questions.q: Which class of Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC / HLA) molecules presents endogenous cytosolic peptides (such as viral or tumor antigens degraded by the immunoproteasome) to CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes?
questions.explain: MHC Class I molecules (composed of a polymorphic alpha heavy chain non-covalently associated with beta-2-microglobulin) are expressed on virtually all nucleated cells, load proteasome-generated peptides via TAP1/TAP2 transporters in the ER, and present them to CD8+ T cells.

open.q: Which class of MHC molecules is recognized by CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes?

questions.q: How does the invariant chain (Ii / CD74) prevent premature binding of endogenous ER peptides to newly synthesized MHC Class II molecules?
options: Phosphorylates the MHC class II peptide-binding groove
CLIP blocks the MHC II groove until HLA-DM exchanges it for antigen peptide
Exports MHC class II to the proteasome
questions.explain: Newly synthesized MHC Class II alpha-beta heterodimers associate with the invariant chain (CD74), whose CLIP segment blocks endogenous peptide binding in the ER; after fusion with endocytic vesicles containing degraded exogenous antigens, HLA-DM catalyzes exchange of CLIP for antigenic peptide.

open.q: Name the peptide fragment of the invariant chain that occupies the MHC Class II binding cleft until exchanged for exogenous antigen peptide by HLA-DM.

questions.q: Which ATP-dependent peptide transporter in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane pumps proteasomal peptide fragments from the cytosol into the ER lumen for loading onto MHC Class I molecules?
options: TAP (Transporter associated with Antigen Processing, TAP1/TAP2)
questions.explain: Deficiency in TAP1 or TAP2 (bare lymphocyte syndrome type I) impairs peptide translocation into the ER, causing unstable empty MHC Class I complexes, low cell-surface MHC Class I expression, and reduced CD8+ T-cell counts.

open.q: State the acronym for the ER membrane peptide transporter (TAP1/TAP2) that imports cytosolic peptides for MHC Class I loading.

questions.q: Which professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs) constitutively express high levels of MHC Class II, costimulatory ligands (CD80/CD86), and perform cross-presentation of exogenous antigens onto MHC Class I?
questions.explain: Dendritic cells are the premier professional APCs that capture antigens in peripheral tissues, migrate to lymph nodes, upregulate CCR7 and CD80/CD86, and activate naive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (including via cross-presentation).

open.q: Name the professional antigen-presenting cell type most potent at activating naive T lymphocytes.

questions.q: Which central complement protein (C3) is cleaved by C3 convertases into C3b (a major opsonin) and C3a (an anaphylatoxin)?
questions.explain: C3 cleavage is the convergence point of the classical, lectin, and alternative complement pathways; surface-bound C3b opsonizes microbes for phagocytosis via CR1/CR3, while C3a and C5a recruit neutrophils and trigger mast cell degranulation.

open.q: Which complement component is cleaved into C3a and C3b at the central hub of all three complement activation pathways?

questions.q: Which terminal complement complex (C5b-9) inserts into target microbial or cell membranes to form a transmembrane pore causing osmotic lysis?
questions.explain: Cleavage of C5 generates C5b, which sequentially recruits C6, C7, C8, and multiple copies of C9 to polymerize into the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b-9) pore.

open.q: Name the terminal cytolytic complement complex (C5b-9) that forms pores in target cell membranes.

questions.q: A 21-year-old woman experiences recurrent episodes of painless, non-pruritic swelling of the lips, eyelids, tongue, hands, and gastrointestinal mucosa (causing severe abdominal pain) that do not respond to antihistamines or epinephrine. Deficiency of which complement regulatory protein causes hereditary angioedema?
questions.explain: C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) regulates both the classical complement pathway (C1r/C1s) and the contact/kallikrein-kinin system; its deficiency leads to uninhibited kallikrein activity and excess bradykinin, causing vascular permeability and angioedema.

open.q: Which vasoactive peptide accumulates due to C1 inhibitor deficiency to cause swelling in hereditary angioedema?

questions.q: Why does paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) cause complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis of red blood cells?
options: Loss of GPI-anchored CD55 and CD59 due to a PIGA mutation
questions.explain: PIGA mutation impairs GPI anchor synthesis, stripping protective GPI-linked CD55 (accelerates decay of C3/C5 convertases) and CD59 (blocks C9 polymerization into MAC) from blood cells, causing intravascular hemolysis, thrombosis, and cytopenias.

open.q: Name the GPI-anchored cell-surface protein that directly inhibits assembly of the terminal membrane attack complex (MAC) by blocking C9 binding.

questions.q: Which complement pathway is antibody-independent and initiated when mannose-binding lectin (MBL) or ficolins bind pathogen surface carbohydrate patterns and activate MBL-associated serine proteases (MASPs)?
questions.explain: The lectin pathway is triggered by microbial mannose/fucose/N-acetylglucosamine arrays bound by MBL or ficolins, activating MASP-1 and MASP-2 to cleave C4 and C2 into the classical-like C3 convertase (C4b2a).

open.q: Name the complement pathway initiated by mannose-binding lectin binding to microbial carbohydrates.

questions.q: How does the alternative complement pathway maintain low-level baseline 'tick-over' activation and amplify C3b deposition on microbial surfaces?
options: Antigen-bound IgG or IgM activates the classical pathway
C3bBb forms spontaneously; properdin stabilises it, while Factors H and I regulate it
Antibodies activate the lectin pathway through C1q
questions.explain: The alternative pathway provides an amplification loop via C3bBb (stabilized by properdin); host cells avoid lysis via sialic acid/polyanion binding of Factor H (cofactor for Factor I cleavage of C3b) and membrane CR1/DAF/MCP.

open.q: Which positive regulator protein stabilizes the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb) on microbial surfaces?

questions.q: In an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), what is the function of the enzyme conjugated to the detection antibody (such as horseradish peroxidase [HRP] or alkaline phosphatase [AP])?
options: Binds directly to the plastic well
Converts substrate into a detectable coloured or fluorescent product
questions.explain: Enzyme amplification enables sensitive spectrophotometric or fluorometric quantification of target antigens (e.g., HIV p24, HBsAg, cytokines) or specific antibodies (e.g., anti-HIV, autoimmune antibodies).

open.q: Name one enzyme commonly conjugated to detection antibodies in ELISA assays.

questions.q: Why is a 'blocking' step (using bovine serum albumin [BSA], casein, or non-fat milk) performed after coating a microtiter plate or blotting membrane in ELISA and Western blotting?
options: Blocks unoccupied surface sites to reduce non-specific antibody binding
questions.explain: Polystyrene ELISA plates and nitrocellulose/PVDF membranes bind proteins non-specifically; blocking saturates free sites so antibodies bind only to the specific immobilized target.

open.q: What is the purpose of adding a blocking agent such as BSA or casein in ELISA and Western blotting?

questions.q: How does a 'sandwich' ELISA differ from an 'indirect' ELISA?
options: Sandwich ELISA detects antigen; indirect ELISA detects patient antibodies
Sandwich ELISA detects only patient antibodies; indirect ELISA measures antigen with two capture antibodies
Both detect nucleic acids using fluorescent probes
Indirect ELISA requires no antigen-antibody binding
questions.explain: Sandwich ELISA excels at quantifying specific antigens in complex fluids (like serum or urine), whereas indirect ELISA is widely used to screen for specific antibodies (such as viral serologies or autoantibodies).

open.q: Which ELISA format uses a surface-bound capture antibody and a second enzyme-linked detection antibody to quantify a specific antigen?

questions.q: In a Western blot (immunoblot) used as a confirmatory test for HIV or Lyme disease, what does it detect after gel electrophoresis and membrane transfer?
options: Specific proteins appear as bands after electrophoresis and membrane transfer
Intact bacteria are visualised by light microscopy
Messenger RNA splice variants are identified
questions.explain: Western blotting separates complex antigen mixtures by SDS-PAGE size, transfers them to a membrane, and probes with patient serum (or specific antibodies) to identify reactivity against individual proteins of defined molecular mass.

open.q: Name the immunoblotting technique used to detect specific proteins or antibodies against individual protein bands separated by gel electrophoresis.

questions.q: What is the principle of a lateral flow immunochromatographic rapid diagnostic test (such as a rapid malaria antigen test, pregnancy hCG test, or HIV rapid test)?
options: Capillary flow carries sample and labelled antibodies across test/control lines
questions.explain: Capillary action moves analyte through a conjugate pad containing antibody-coated gold/latex nanoparticles toward immobilized capture antibodies at the Test line and anti-species antibodies at the Control line.

open.q: On a lateral flow rapid diagnostic strip test, what does appearance of the Control (C) line verify?
accept: Proper fluid flow and functional test reagents

questions.q: How does flow cytometry analyze individual cells in suspension stained with fluorochrome-conjugated monoclonal antibodies?
options: Laser-based single-cell analysis of light scatter and fluorescence
Cells are separated by molecular weight in a gel
Antibody charge is measured in a capillary
Cells are counted only by light microscopy
questions.explain: Flow cytometry measures thousands of single cells per second using forward scatter (size), side scatter (granularity), and multi-color fluorescence (immunophenotyping CD markers in leukemias, lymphomas, and HIV CD4 counts).

open.q: In flow cytometry, what does forward scatter (FSC) primarily correlate with?

questions.q: How does direct immunofluorescence differ from indirect immunofluorescence?
options: Direct immunofluorescence uses a single fluorophore-conjugated primary antibody specific for the target antigen, whereas indirect immunofluorescence uses an unlabeled primary antibody followed by a fluorophore-conjugated secondary antibody (providing signal amplification)
Indirect immunofluorescence cannot use fluorescent dyes
questions.explain: Indirect immunofluorescence amplifies signal because multiple fluorophore-labeled secondary antibodies can bind a single primary antibody, and it avoids labeling every primary antibody (e.g., used in antinuclear antibody [ANA] testing on HEp-2 cells).

open.q: Why does indirect immunofluorescence generally provide greater sensitivity than direct immunofluorescence?
accept: Signal amplification by multiple labeled secondary antibodies

questions.q: In Kohler and Milstein's hybridoma technology for generating monoclonal antibodies, why are fused hybridoma cells grown in HAT (hypoxanthine-aminopterin-thymidine) selection medium?
options: Hybridomas survive via B-cell HGPRT salvage activity and myeloma immortality
It selects the highest-affinity IgG without cell fusion
It allows HGPRT-deficient myeloma cells to survive
It induces class switching in unfused myeloma cells
questions.explain: HGPRT-deficient myeloma cells cannot use hypoxanthine/thymidine when aminopterin blocks de novo purine/pyrimidine synthesis, whereas primary B cells have a short lifespan in culture; hybridomas combine B-cell HGPRT with myeloma immortality.

open.q: Which salvage pathway enzyme is deficient in the myeloma fusion partner used in HAT selection during hybridoma generation?

questions.q: How do chimeric, humanized, and fully human monoclonal antibodies differ in sequence composition and immunogenicity (HAMA response)?
options: Chimeric: mouse variable/human constant; humanised: mainly mouse CDRs; fully human: human sequence
Chimeric: fully human; humanised: fully mouse; fully human: mouse variable/human constant
Chimeric: mouse constant/human variable; humanised: human CDRs only; fully human: mouse framework
All three formats have identical sequences and immunogenicity
questions.explain: Reducing non-human sequence from chimeric (-ximab) to humanized (-zumab) to fully human (-umab) decreases human anti-mouse antibody (HAMA) responses, prolongs half-life, and improves Fc effector compatibility. Chimeric antibodies combine mouse variable regions with human constant regions; humanised antibodies retain mainly the mouse antigen-binding CDRs on a human framework; fully human antibodies have human sequences. In general, reducing non-human sequence reduces immunogenicity.

open.q: In a humanized monoclonal antibody, which antigen-contacting loops from the non-human antibody are grafted onto a human antibody framework?

questions.q: How do immune checkpoint inhibitor monoclonal antibodies such as pembrolizumab or nivolumab (anti-PD-1) and ipilimumab (anti-CTLA-4) enhance anti-tumor immunity?
options: Block inhibitory T-cell checkpoints, restoring anti-tumour T-cell activity
questions.explain: Tumors often upregulate PD-L1 to engage PD-1 on tumor-infiltrating T cells and induce T-cell exhaustion; blocking PD-1 or CTLA-4 restores T-cell proliferation and effector function.

open.q: Which T-cell inhibitory receptor is targeted by pembrolizumab and nivolumab?

questions.q: What is Antibody-Dependent Cellular Cytotoxicity (ADCC) mediated by therapeutic IgG1 monoclonal antibodies such as trastuzumab (anti-HER2) or rituximab (anti-CD20)?
options: IgG1 Fc binds NK-cell CD16, triggering perforin/granzyme release
IgG1 blocks all glucose uptake in the target cell
NK cells recognise the antigen directly without antibody
ADCC occurs only without Fc receptors
questions.explain: NK cells express activating Fc-gamma-RIIIa (CD16) and recognize antibody-coated target cells, releasing perforin and granzymes (and Fas ligand) to kill opsonized tumor or infected cells.

open.q: Which cytotoxic lymphocyte population primarily mediates Antibody-Dependent Cellular Cytotoxicity (ADCC) via Fc-gamma-RIIIa (CD16)?

questions.q: In a quantitative precipitin curve (Heidelberger curve) mixing a fixed amount of antibody with increasing concentrations of soluble multivalent antigen, what occurs in the 'prozone' (antibody excess) and 'postzone' (antigen excess) compared with the 'zone of equivalence'?
options: Precipitation peaks at equivalence; antigen or antibody excess prevents lattice formation
Precipitation is greatest in extreme antigen excess
Lattice formation occurs only in postzone
Antibodies precipitate without antigen in prozone
questions.explain: Multivalent cross-linking requires balanced proportions of multivalent antigen and bivalent/multivalent antibody (equivalence zone); excess antibody saturates individual antigen sites while excess antigen saturates individual antibody sites, preventing large lattice formation.

open.q: In an antigen-antibody precipitation reaction, what region yields the largest amount of insoluble cross-linked immune precipitate?

questions.q: How do agglutination assays differ from precipitation assays in immunochemistry?
options: Agglutination clumps particles; precipitation forms complexes from soluble antigens
Precipitation uses red cells, whereas agglutination uses soluble proteins
questions.explain: Agglutination is widely used in ABO/Rh blood typing, Coombs (antiglobulin) tests, and latex agglutination assays because clumping of particles is visually obvious at low analyte concentrations.

open.q: What term describes the clumping of particulate antigens (such as erythrocytes or antibody-coated latex beads) cross-linked by antibodies?

questions.q: How do nephelometry and turbidimetry quantify specific serum proteins (such as C-reactive protein, immunoglobulins, or complement C3/C4) formed into immune complexes?
options: Nephelometry detects scattered light; turbidimetry detects reduced transmitted light
Both measure electrical conductivity of urine
questions.explain: Immune complexes scatter incident light; nephelometry detects scattered light off-axis (high sensitivity at low concentrations), while turbidimetry detects decreased transmitted light along the incident beam.

open.q: Which optical method measures light scattered at an angle by antigen-antibody complexes in solution?

questions.q: What are Bence Jones proteins detected in serum or urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation in multiple myeloma?
options: Free monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains excreted in urine
questions.explain: In multiple myeloma (malignant plasma cell dyscrasia), monoclonal plasma cells often secrete excess free kappa or lambda light chains (~22-25 kDa) that pass through the glomerulus and appear as Bence Jones proteinuria (classically precipitating upon heating to ~40-60 C and redissolving near 100 C, though immunofixation is the diagnostic standard).

open.q: What type of immunoglobulin polypeptide are Bence Jones proteins?

questions.q: How does the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) extend the serum half-life of IgG and albumin?
options: FcRn binds IgG/albumin in acidic endosomes and recycles them
FcRn synthesises IgG and albumin in endothelial cells
FcRn cleaves IgG into Fab and Fc fragments
FcRn prevents IgG from binding antigen
questions.explain: pH-dependent binding to FcRn (high affinity at acidic endosomal pH ~6.0, release at physiological pH ~7.4) rescues IgG and albumin from catabolism, giving IgG1, IgG2, and IgG4 a ~3-week half-life (whereas IgG3 lacks high-affinity FcRn binding and has a ~7-day half-life).

open.q: State the acronym for the neonatal Fc receptor responsible for recycling IgG and extending its serum half-life.

questions.q: What is the structural difference between MHC Class I and MHC Class II peptide-binding grooves that determines the length of peptides each can bind?
options: MHC I has a closed-ended groove for short peptides; MHC II has an open-ended groove that accommodates longer peptides
MHC I binds long peptides in an open groove; MHC II binds short peptides in a closed groove
Both classes have identical grooves and bind peptides of the same length
MHC I binds carbohydrates, whereas MHC II binds lipids
questions.explain: Because the MHC Class I cleft is closed at both ends, peptides typically bulge slightly and measure 8-10 residues, whereas the open-ended MHC Class II cleft allows longer peptides to extend out of both ends.

open.q: Typical peptides bound by MHC Class I molecules are generally how many amino acids long?

questions.q: Why are HLA (MHC) genes described as the most polymorphic genes in the human genome, and what is codominant expression?
options: Numerous allelic variants exist across the population (maximizing peptide repertoire coverage across individuals), and codominant expression means an individual expresses both maternal and paternal HLA alleles simultaneously on their cells
Each person inherits only one HLA allele for life
HLA genes do not vary between individuals
Only one parental allele is expressed in any cell
questions.explain: Extreme polymorphism at HLA-A, -B, -C, -DP, -DQ, and -DR combined with codominant expression of both parental haplotypes broadens the range of pathogen peptides a person can present to T cells (though it also drives transplantation rejection).

open.q: What term describes simultaneous cell-surface expression of both maternal and paternal alleles of MHC/HLA genes?

questions.q: Which anaphylatoxin is the most potent mediator of neutrophil chemotaxis, vascular permeability, and mast cell degranulation among complement cleavage fragments?
questions.explain: C5a is a potent anaphylatoxin and chemotactic factor for neutrophils and monocytes via C5aR1, whereas C3a has weaker anaphylatoxic activity and C3b functions primarily as an opsonin.

open.q: Which complement split product is the most potent anaphylatoxin and neutrophil chemoattractant?

questions.q: In a direct Coombs test (direct antiglobulin test, DAT), what is being detected on the surface of a patient's red blood cells?
options: IgG and/or complement bound to the patient's red cells in vivo
questions.explain: Adding anti-human globulin (Coombs reagent) to washed patient RBCs causes agglutination if IgG or complement is already bound to the RBC surface in vivo (direct Coombs); the indirect Coombs test detects unbound anti-RBC antibodies in serum.

open.q: What reagent causes agglutination in a positive direct Coombs test when IgG or complement is bound to patient red blood cells?

questions.q: What is the 'hook effect' (prozone phenomenon in immunometric/sandwich assays) when an analyte such as hCG or prolactin is present at extremely high concentration?
options: Excess antigen saturates both assay antibodies, causing a falsely low signal
Antibodies bind to glass instead of plastic
Substrate concentration permanently exceeds enzyme Vmax
The sample temperature falls below 0 C
questions.explain: At very high antigen concentrations in a one-step sandwich assay, excess antigen independently saturates capture and tracer antibodies, preventing sandwich formation and causing a falsely depressed reading unless the sample is diluted.

open.q: How is a falsely low result caused by the hook effect in an immunoassay resolved?

questions.q: What is a bispecific T-cell engager (BiTE) or bispecific monoclonal antibody?
options: Engineered antibody with two binding specificities, e.g. CD3 and tumour antigen
An antibody binding two identical epitopes on one monomer
A complement inhibitor blocking C1 and C9
questions.explain: Bispecific antibodies bridge two different targets simultaneously, such as recruiting CD3+ T cells directly to tumor cells to trigger T-cell activation and target lysis.

open.q: Which T-cell surface complex is commonly targeted alongside a tumor antigen by T-cell-engaging bispecific antibodies?

questions.q: In radial immunodiffusion (Mancini assay), how is the concentration of an antigen (such as a specific serum immunoglobulin) determined?
options: Antigen diffuses into antibody gel; ring diameter squared reflects concentration
White cells are counted by impedance
questions.explain: In radial immunodiffusion, antigen diffuses outward into antibody-impregnated gel until equivalence is reached; ring area (proportional to diameter squared) correlates linearly with antigen concentration.

open.q: In radial immunodiffusion, antigen concentration is proportional to the precipitin ring's diameter or diameter squared?

questions.q: Which variable regions of an immunoglobulin heavy and light chain form the hypervariable complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) that directly contact the antigen epitope?
options: Three hypervariable loops (CDR1–3) in each variable domain
questions.explain: Each variable domain (VH and VL) contains three hypervariable CDR loops (six CDRs per Fab arm) that assemble at the tip of the Fab to create the antigen-binding site (paratope).

open.q: State the acronym for the three hypervariable loops in each immunoglobulin variable domain that form the antigen-binding surface.
